title: Fibonacci Heap Amortised Decrease-Key
subject: Data Structures
statement: A Fibonacci heap supports insert, meld and decrease-key in O(1) amortised time and extract-min in O(log n) amortised time.
short: Lazy restructuring postpones work until a delete-min forces consolidation.
long: Lazy restructuring postpones work until a delete-min forces consolidation. Decrease-key cuts a node and may cascade cuts up the tree; the potential stored in marked nodes pays for them.
proof: The potential is the number of trees plus twice the number of marked nodes; consolidation and cascading cuts are charged against it.
consequence: It improves Dijkstra and Prim on dense graphs to O(E + V log V) amortised.

title: Pairing Heap Practical Performance
subject: Data Structures
statement: Pairing heaps are simple multiary meldable heaps that perform very well in practice despite lacking a tight amortised proof for all operations.
short: Elegant in code, resisted exact analysis for years.
long: Elegant in code, resisted exact analysis for years. Meld is a pointer comparison and extract-min merges children in two passes; known upper bounds are close to but not exactly O(log n).
proof: Meld of two heaps simply compares roots and attaches the smaller under the larger, a constant-time operation.
consequence: They are a common pragmatic choice when meldable heaps are needed and worst-case bounds are not critical.

title: van Emde Boas Tree for Small Universes
subject: Data Structures
statement: A van Emde Boas tree supports predecessor, successor, insert and delete on a universe of size u in O(log log u) time.
short: Recursive sqrt-sized summaries give doubly logarithmic depth.
long: Recursive sqrt-sized summaries give doubly logarithmic depth. It uses O(u) space and is fastest when the key universe is modest, such as machine words or small integers.
proof: Splitting the universe into sqrt(u) clusters and recursing on a summary gives T(u)=T(sqrt u)+O(1), hence log log u.
consequence: It breaks the log n comparison barrier for integer keys by exploiting the bounded universe.

title: Y-Fast Trie Reduces vEB Space
subject: Data Structures
statement: A y-fast trie stores n keys from a u-element universe in O(n) space with expected O(log log u) predecessor searches.
short: Buckets of balanced trees mimic a vEB tree with linear space.
long: Buckets of balanced trees mimic a vEB tree with linear space. Each bucket holds O(log u) keys in a balanced tree; a hash table maps bucket representatives.
proof: A vEB tree on the O(n/log u) bucket representatives plus local tree search gives the stated bound.
consequence: It gives near-vEB speed with linear storage, important for large integer universes.

title: Binary Trie for Integer Keys
subject: Data Structures
statement: A binary trie on fixed-width integer keys branches on successive bits, supporting insert, lookup and predecessor in O(w) time for word size w.
short: Bit-level branching gives a bounded-depth tree.
long: Bit-level branching gives a bounded-depth tree. With 32- or 64-bit keys the depth is a machine constant, making tries competitive with hashing.
proof: Each key has exactly w bits, so any search traverses at most w levels.
consequence: Binary tries underlie IP longest-prefix matching and compressed integer indexes.

title: Interval Tree for Overlap Queries
subject: Data Structures
statement: An interval tree stores intervals in a balanced tree keyed by left endpoint with augmented maximum right endpoints, reporting all overlaps in O(log n + k) time.
short: Augmented maxima prune branches that cannot overlap.
long: Augmented maxima prune branches that cannot overlap. The max-right field at each node tells whether any interval in a subtree can intersect the query.
proof: Search both children only when their maximum right endpoint exceeds the query's left endpoint, charging visited nodes to output or path length.
consequence: Interval trees are used in calendar scheduling, computational geometry and compiler register allocation.

title: Quadtree Hierarchical Space Partition
subject: Data Structures
statement: A quadtree recursively subdivides two-dimensional space into four quadrants, storing points or occupancy in the leaves.
short: Spatial subdivision makes region queries local.
long: Spatial subdivision makes region queries local. Point quadtrees split at points, region quadtrees split at geometric midlines; depth depends on point distribution.
proof: Each subdivision reduces the region size by half, so a point is stored at depth proportional to its coordinate precision.
consequence: Quadtrees support spatial indexing, image compression and collision detection.

title: k-d Tree Average-Case Nearest Neighbour
subject: Data Structures
statement: A k-d tree recursively splits points by alternating coordinate axes, giving O(log n) expected nearest-neighbour search for well-distributed points and O(n) worst case.
short: Axis-aligned splits prune most of space on typical data.
long: Axis-aligned splits prune most of space on typical data. Range queries in two dimensions take O(sqrt(n)+k) expected time for balanced random data.
proof: A balanced split halves the point set each level, so the query follows one branch with occasional backtracking.
consequence: k-d trees are a simple baseline for low-dimensional nearest-neighbour search, though curse of dimensionality hurts high dimensions.

title: Priority Queue as an Abstract Data Type
subject: Data Structures
statement: A priority queue supports insert and extract-min (or extract-max) on items with comparable keys, independent of any particular implementation.
short: Order by priority, not by arrival time.
long: Order by priority, not by arrival time. Common implementations are binary heaps (O(log n) worst case), Fibonacci heaps (amortised improvements) and balanced trees.
proof: The ADT is specified by its operations and their effect on the multiset of keys, not by storage details.
consequence: It is the key abstraction behind Dijkstra, Prim, Huffman coding and event-driven simulation.

title: Heap versus Balanced Tree for Priority Queues
subject: Data Structures
statement: A heap is smaller and faster for pure priority-queue operations, while a balanced tree supports ordered queries such as predecessor and range scan.
short: Choose by which operations you need, not by asymptotic equality.
long: Choose by which operations you need, not by asymptotic equality. Heaps lack efficient arbitrary delete or search by key; trees pay extra pointer and rotation overhead.
proof: Both maintain logarithmic height, but trees additionally preserve a total key order across all nodes.
consequence: Dijkstra typically uses a heap; an ordered set of active keys requires a tree.

title: Move-to-Front Self-Organising List
subject: Data Structures
statement: Move-to-front moves a requested item to the head of an unstructured list, giving competitive performance on sequences with locality.
short: Temporal locality is exploited without knowing access probabilities.
long: Temporal locality is exploited without knowing access probabilities. Its competitive ratio against the optimal static ordering is at most 2, and it matches the optimal offline cost up to a constant factor.
proof: An element pays at most one extra move per other element moved ahead of it, giving constant competitiveness via a potential argument.
consequence: The idea appears in caching heuristics and entropy coding transforms.

title: LRU Cache with Hash Map and Doubly Linked List
subject: Data Structures
statement: A hash map to nodes plus a doubly linked list in recency order supports get and put in O(1) expected time.
short: Hashing finds the node, list order tracks recency.
long: Hashing finds the node, list order tracks recency. On access the node is spliced to the front; on overflow the tail is evicted.
proof: Map lookups are expected constant and list splicing uses stored predecessor/successor pointers.
consequence: This is the canonical implementation of least-recently-used caches in operating systems and databases.

title: Persistent Stack by Node Sharing
subject: Data Structures
statement: A persistent stack allocates a new head node on push and shares the unchanged tail, so old versions remain accessible in O(1) time and space per update.
short: Immutable nodes let versions share structure.
long: Immutable nodes let versions share structure. Persistence can be partial (only newest version updated) or full (all versions updated); here updates return a new stack.
proof: A new node points to the old head, so both versions are valid linked lists with no mutation of shared nodes.
consequence: Persistent structures underpin functional programming, undo mechanisms and versioned indexes.

title: CSR Compressed Sparse Matrix Format
subject: Data Structures
statement: Compressed sparse row stores nonzero values, their column indices and row-start offsets in three arrays.
short: Only nonzeros are stored, with row boundaries recorded.
long: Only nonzeros are stored, with row boundaries recorded. Matrix-vector multiplication takes O(nnz) time; random element access is slower than in dense format.
proof: Row pointers delimit contiguous slices of values and column indices for each row.
consequence: CSR is the standard sparse-matrix format in scientific computing and graph algorithms.

title: Adjacency List versus Adjacency Matrix
subject: Data Structures
statement: Adjacency lists use O(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours in O(deg v), while adjacency matrices use O(V^2) space and test edge existence in O(1).
short: Sparse graphs favour lists; dense graphs favour matrices.
long: Sparse graphs favour lists; dense graphs favour matrices. Traversal with a matrix costs O(V^2) even for sparse graphs, while repeated edge queries favour matrices.
proof: Lists store each edge once, matrices store one bit per ordered pair.
consequence: Choosing the representation often dominates the practical cost of graph algorithms.

title: Structure of Arrays Improves Cache Use
subject: Data Structures
statement: Storing each field in a separate contiguous array can speed up kernels that access only one field, compared with an array of records.
short: Fetch only the bytes the kernel actually reads.
long: Fetch only the bytes the kernel actually reads. It improves spatial locality and enables vectorisation, but hurts when all fields of a record are needed together.
proof: Cache lines then contain only useful field values rather than interleaved unused bytes.
consequence: SoA layout is common in high-performance graphics, physics and columnar databases.

title: Linked Structure Memory Locality Penalty
subject: Data Structures
statement: Pointer-based structures can be asymptotically optimal yet slower than arrays because each node may cause a cache miss.
latex: O(1)\ pointers,\ O(1)\ cache\ miss\ each
short: Big-O hides the cost of chasing pointers through memory.
long: Big-O hides the cost of chasing pointers through memory. A pointer-rich tree or list scatters allocations, while an array-backed heap or open-addressed table prefetches well.
proof: Each node dereference may map to a different cache line, and cache misses dominate arithmetic on modern hardware.
consequence: Cache-aware design sometimes prefers arrays and implicit indices over elegant pointer structures.

title: Amortised Cost of Repeated Minimum Extraction
subject: Data Structures
statement: Repeatedly extracting the minimum from a heap built once costs O(n log n) total, since the build is linear and each of n extractions costs O(log n).
short: Build once, then pay only for the extractions.
long: Build once, then pay only for the extractions. This is the exact cost profile of heapsort's selection phase.
proof: Linearity of the build plus the heap height bound on each extraction gives the total.
consequence: It explains why heapsort matches merge sort asymptotically without extra space.

title: Union-Find in Online Connected Components
subject: Data Structures
statement: Processing edges in any order and unioning endpoints maintains connected components of an undirected graph incrementally.
short: Union-find answers connectivity as edges arrive.
long: Union-find answers connectivity as edges arrive. It cannot handle deletions, which require dynamic connectivity structures.
proof: The equivalence relation generated by processed edges is exactly connectivity in the graph of those edges.
consequence: This is the standard fast path for Kruskal's algorithm and percolation simulations.

title: Try-and-Error Search Versus Dictionary Lookup
subject: Data Structures
statement: Searching among n items by checking membership in a hash table takes expected O(1) per probe, but finding an unknown key still requires n probes in the worst case.
short: Fast membership does not replace a search problem.
long: Fast membership does not replace a search problem. A hash table answers 'is x present?' instantly but cannot list nearby keys or discover a target without a candidate.
proof: Without order or a candidate-generation rule, at least one probe per possible key may be needed.
consequence: Dictionaries accelerate verification, not discovery; ordered indexes are needed for range search.

title: Comparison Sorting Lower Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case to sort n distinct items.
short: There are n! possible orders and each comparison is binary.
long: There are n! possible orders and each comparison is binary. The bound holds regardless of implementation tricks, but non-comparison sorts can beat it for restricted key types.
proof: A decision tree with n! leaves has depth at least log2(n!) = Omega(n log n) by Stirling's formula.
consequence: Merge sort, heapsort and introsort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts.

title: Decision Tree Model for Sorting
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: In the decision tree model each internal node is a comparison between two keys, each branch is an outcome, and each leaf is a permutation.
short: Sorting is a game of twenty questions over permutations.
long: Sorting is a game of twenty questions over permutations. The model ignores arithmetic on keys, which is precisely why it does not apply to counting or radix sort.
proof: Every possible input ordering must reach a distinct leaf, so the tree must have at least n! leaves.
consequence: This model supplies the standard optimality proof for comparison sorts.

title: Insertion Sort and Its Costs
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix by shifting larger elements right; it is O(n^2) worst and average case, O(n) best case, uses O(1) extra space and is stable.
short: Simple, stable and fast on small or nearly sorted arrays.
long: Simple, stable and fast on small or nearly sorted arrays. It is often used as the base case for quicker recursive sorts.
proof: Shifting costs O(i) for the i-th element, summing to O(n^2); equal keys are never swapped past each other.
consequence: Its stability and low overhead make it the standard small-subarray routine in hybrid sorts.

title: Insertion Sort Adaptive Bound by Inversions
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Insertion sort runs in Theta(n + I) time where I is the number of inversions in the input.
short: Nearly sorted inputs with few inversions finish almost linearly.
long: Nearly sorted inputs with few inversions finish almost linearly. This is a precise adaptivity measure: an already sorted array has I = 0 and costs linear time.
proof: Each shift removes exactly one inversion, and each element requires at least one comparison.
consequence: It explains why insertion sort outperforms asymptotically better algorithms on small perturbations.

title: Selection Sort Trade-off
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted suffix and swaps it into place, taking Theta(n^2) time and O(1) space.
short: Minimal writes, quadratic comparisons.
long: Minimal writes, quadratic comparisons. The straightforward version is not stable because a swap can move an equal element past another.
proof: Finding the minimum of a suffix of size k costs k-1 comparisons, giving n(n-1)/2 comparisons in total.
consequence: It is useful when writes are expensive, but dominated on speed by insertion or heap sort.
